extracted.intended_audience: students of the Catholic catechism / children receiving basic religious instruction
extracted.subtask_description: A question-and-answer catechism lesson presenting fundamental Catholic doctrines (creation, nature of God, the soul, Trinity, angels) with explanatory guidance and examples for young learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who made the world?
rubrics_metrics.description: God made the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'world' here is explained to mean the whole universe — sun, moon, stars, and everything seen now or that may be seen in the future with instruments. (Q&A 1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is God?
rubrics_metrics.description: God is the Creator of Heaven and earth, and of all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms God's role as Creator of all that exists. (Q&A 2)

rubrics_metrics.name: What is man?
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is a creature composed of a body and soul, and made to the image and likeness of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that man uniquely combines spirit and matter (soul and body) distinguishing him from beings that are purely material or purely spiritual. (Q&A 3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Is this likeness in the body or in the soul?
rubrics_metrics.description: This likeness is chiefly in the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the essential likeness to God resides primarily in the soul rather than the body. (Q&A 4)

rubrics_metrics.name: How is the soul like to God?
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is like God because it is a spirit that will never die, and has understanding and free will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text specifies four aspects: (1) it is a spirit (invisible but real); (2) it is immortal (will never cease to exist); (3) it has understanding (reason) enabling reflection and foresight; (4) it has free will, allowing choice and moral responsibility. Each aspect is illustrated (e.g., spirit compared with wind/electricity; free will contrasted with animal instinct). (Q&A 5 and expanded explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: My soul is a spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul really exists though it cannot be seen with bodily eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains invisible things (wind, electricity) as analogies showing invisibility does not negate real existence. (Part of Q&A 5 explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: My soul is immortal
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul will never die; it lasts as long as God Himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stresses the permanence of the soul. (Part of Q&A 5 explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: My soul has understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul has the gift of reason enabling reflection on actions and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates human reason from animal instinct; uses examples of human progress vs. animal repetition to show reason. Notes that reason alone cannot discover all truths (some require Revelation). (Part of Q&A 5 explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: My soul has free will
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul can choose to do or not do a thing; free will makes moral praise or blame possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains moral responsibility depends on freedom; gives examples (starving despite food available; Daniel in the lions' den as miracle-exception showing divine intervention). (Part of Q&A 5 explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Why did God make you?
rubrics_metrics.description: God made me to know Him, to love Him, and to serve Him in this world, and to be happy with Him forever in the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the order: to know God (so we may love Him), to love, and then to serve Him; encourages further learning (catechism, sermons, books) and notes conduct in this life determines condition in the next. (Q&A 6 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Of which must we take more care, our soul or our body?
rubrics_metrics.description: We must take more care of our soul than of our body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues we should preserve the more valuable thing (soul) even at cost to the body; uses analogies (pocket-book with money, kite and tail). (Q&A 7 and 8)

rubrics_metrics.name: What must we do to save our souls?
rubrics_metrics.description: To save our souls, we must worship God by faith, hope, and charity; that is, believe in Him, hope in Him, and love Him with all our heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'worship' as giving divine honor; distinguishes three kinds of veneration used by theologians—latria (supreme worship to God), dulia (veneration of saints), hyperdulia (special veneration of the Blessed Virgin)—and explains practical signs of loving God (readiness to obey God above all, willingness to offend others rather than God). (Q&A 9 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: How shall we know the things which we are to believe?
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall know the things which we are to believe from the Catholic Church, through which God speaks to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the Church as Pope, councils, bishops, and priests who teach in the Church. Appeals to ecclesial authority as source of revealed truths. (Q&A 10)

rubrics_metrics.name: Where shall we find the chief truths which the Catholic Church teaches?
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall find the chief truths which the Catholic Church teaches in the Apostles' Creed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the Apostles' Creed contains the 'chief' (but not all) truths; gives examples of doctrines not explicitly in the Creed (Eucharist, Immaculate Conception, papal infallibility). (Q&A 11 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostles' Creed (text)
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe in God, the Father Almighty, Creator of Heaven and earth; and in Jesus Christ... and the life everlasting. Amen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the full text of the Apostles' Creed and brief lexical notes (e.g., 'descend' means go down). (Q&A 12)

rubrics_metrics.name: What is God? (perfections)
rubrics_metrics.description: God is a spirit infinitely perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'spirit' as living, intelligent, invisible; 'infinitely perfect' means possessing all perfections without limit (wisdom, power, goodness, beauty), and that created perfections are only loans from God. 'Perfect' means without defect. (Q&A 13)

rubrics_metrics.name: Had God a beginning?
rubrics_metrics.description: God had no beginning; He always was and always will be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts God's eternal existence; calls it a mystery to be explained later. (Q&A 14)

rubrics_metrics.name: Where is God?
rubrics_metrics.description: God is everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies not as spread out but whole and entire in every place; uses the cannon report simile to illustrate how one thing can be fully present to many observers. (Q&A 15 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: If God is everywhere, why do we not see Him?
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not see God because He is a pure spirit and cannot be seen with bodily eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterates 'pure spirit' meaning not clothed with material body. (Q&A 16)

rubrics_metrics.name: Does God see us?
rubrics_metrics.description: God sees us and watches over us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'watches' as protecting, rewarding, or punishing; God preserves us moment by moment. Uses analogy of a man hanging by a rope over a precipice to emphasize dependence and folly of sinning against God. (Q&A 17 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Does God know all things?
rubrics_metrics.description: God knows all things, even our most secret thoughts, words, and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues God's omniscience by His infinite wisdom and omnipresence; warns that secret sins are known and will be revealed on the last day. (Q&A 18 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Can God do all things?
rubrics_metrics.description: God can do all things, and nothing is hard or impossible to Him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms divine omnipotence. (Q&A 19)

rubrics_metrics.name: Is God just, holy, and merciful?
rubrics_metrics.description: God is all just, all holy, all merciful, as He is infinitely perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'just' (gives everyone what belongs to them), 'holy' (good), 'merciful' (compassionate, forgiving). Uses judge analogy to explain balance of justice and mercy; asserts God must punish sin as He has promised. (Q&A 20 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there but one God?
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes; there is but one God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms monotheism. (Q&A 21)

rubrics_metrics.name: Why can there be but one God?
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be but one God because God, being supreme and infinite, cannot have an equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'supreme' and gives analogies about leadership (cannot have two chiefs). Argues all power and authority come from God, so disobeying superiors is disobeying God. (Q&A 22 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: How many persons are there in God?
rubrics_metrics.description: In God there are three divine persons really distinct and equal in all things—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces the doctrine of the Trinity: three distinct persons yet one God; explains terminology (Father, Son) and notes mystery and equality of persons. (Q&A 23)

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the Father God?
rubrics_metrics.description: The Father is God and the first Person of the Blessed Trinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms the divine status of the Father within the Trinity. (Q&A 24)

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the Son God?
rubrics_metrics.description: The Son is God and the second Person of the Blessed Trinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms the divine status of the Son (Jesus Christ). (Q&A 25)

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the Holy Ghost God?
rubrics_metrics.description: The Holy Ghost is God and the third Person of the Blessed Trinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms the divine status of the Holy Spirit. (Q&A 26)

rubrics_metrics.name: What do you mean by the Blessed Trinity?
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Blessed Trinity I mean one God in three Divine Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the Trinity concisely. (Q&A 27)

rubrics_metrics.name: Are the three Divine Persons equal in all things?
rubrics_metrics.description: The three Divine Persons are equal in all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms equality of persons within the Trinity. (Q&A 28)

rubrics_metrics.name: Are the three Divine Persons one and the same God?
rubrics_metrics.description: The three Divine Persons are one and the same God, having one and the same divine nature and substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that although different works are sometimes attributed to different Persons (creation to Father, mercy to Son, sanctification to Holy Ghost), all works are works of one God because there is one divine nature. (Q&A 29 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Can we fully understand the Trinity?
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot fully understand how the three Divine Persons are one and the same God, because this is a mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'mystery' as a revealed truth we cannot fully comprehend and gives analogies (earth's roundness despite sense impressions) to show we must believe on authority when understanding is limited. (Q&A 30 and 31)

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a mystery?
rubrics_metrics.description: A mystery is a truth which we cannot fully understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that mysteries are revealed truths we must accept on authority; gives examples demonstrating belief beyond immediate comprehension. (Q&A 31)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who created Heaven and earth, and all things?
rubrics_metrics.description: God created Heaven and earth, and all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasserts divine creation. (Q&A 32)

rubrics_metrics.name: How did God create Heaven and earth?
rubrics_metrics.description: God created Heaven and earth from nothing, by His word only; that is, by a single act of His all-powerful will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms creation ex nihilo by divine fiat. (Q&A 33)

rubrics_metrics.name: Which are the chief creatures of God?
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief creatures of God are angels and men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes angels (pure spirits) and men (spirit + body) as highest creatures. (Q&A 34)

rubrics_metrics.name: What are angels?
rubrics_metrics.description: Angels are pure spirits without a body, created to adore and enjoy God in Heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains angels differ from saints, lists nine choirs of angels (angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, seraphim), and gives examples of archangels' roles (Michael, Gabriel). (Q&A 35 and explanation)

rubrics_metrics.name: Were the angels created for any other purpose?
rubrics_metrics.description: The angels were also created to assist before the throne of God and to minister unto Him; they have often been sent as messengers from God to man; and are also appointed our guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expands on angelic duties: some remain in Heaven, some are sent as guardians; every person has a guardian angel who prays for and exhorts them. Uses the story of Tobias (angel Raphael) to illustrate angels carrying prayers to God and ministering to humans. (Q&A 36 and extended narrative)
